title: Place Value Grade 3 to 10000: Thousands, Hundreds, Tens and Ones + Free Quiz
meta_title: Place Value Grade 3 to 10000 (4-Digit) + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach place value grade 3 to 10000 the easy way: thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, expanded form and the Indian comma, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Once a child can read 3,458 and tell you the 4 is really 400, four-digit numbers stop being scary. Here is how I teach place value up to 10,000 in Grade 3, plus a quick quiz to check it stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 3,458 on a page and ask a Grade 3 child what the 4 means. If the answer is ‘four,’ you have found the exact gap this lesson fills. The 4 is not four — it is four hundred. That single idea, that a digit’s worth depends on where it sits, is the whole of place value grade 3 to 10000, and it is the foundation for every big-number sum, comparison and word problem that comes after.

In Grade 2 most children learned three-digit numbers: hundreds, tens and ones. Grade 3 adds one column on the left — the thousands — and stretches numbers all the way to 10,000. It sounds like a small step. In practice, that new column is where children stumble, because they have to keep four places straight and not let a digit ‘slide.’ Here is how I teach it so it sticks.

The four places: thousands, hundreds, tens and ones

A four-digit number has exactly four homes for digits. Reading from the right: ones, then tens, then hundreds, then thousands. Each place is ten times the one to its right — ten ones make a ten, ten tens make a hundred, ten hundreds make a thousand. That ‘ten of these makes one of those’ rule is the engine of the whole system, and it is worth saying out loud until a child can finish the sentence for you.

Take 3,458. The 3 sits in the thousands place, so it is worth 3,000. The 4 is in the hundreds, worth 400. The 5 is in the tens, worth 50. The 8 is in the ones, worth 8. Same four digits, four completely different values — that is the point.

The value of a digit by its place

This is the idea children find slippery, so I drill it with the same number written twice. In 5,200 the 5 means 5,000. In 2,500 the same digit 5 means 500. Nothing about the digit changed — only its seat at the table. I like to ask, ‘What is the 7 worth?’ about a fresh number every day for a week: in 7,041 it is 7,000; in 1,700 it is 700; in 4,027 it is only 7.

A quick caveat from the classroom: zero causes more trouble here than any other digit. In 4,027 that 0 is not doing nothing — it is holding the hundreds place open so the 7 stays in the tens. Drop the 0 and you get 427, a different number entirely. Zero is a placeholder, and Grade 3 is exactly when that job needs naming.

Expanded form: pulling a number apart

Expanded form is place value made visible. You write a number as the sum of what each digit is worth:

  • 3,458 = 3000 + 400 + 50 + 8
  • 6,205 = 6000 + 200 + 0 + 5, which we usually shorten to 6000 + 200 + 5
  • 9,090 = 9000 + 0 + 90 + 0, or simply 9000 + 90

Going the other way — from 7000 + 300 + 20 + 4 back to 7,324 — is just as important, and honestly a bit harder for most children. Practise both directions. Expanded form is not busywork; it is the bridge to column addition, where those same thousands, hundreds, tens and ones line up and get added separately.

Reading and writing four-digit numbers

Reading a number is really reading its places in order. For 3,458 you say ‘three thousand, four hundred and fifty-eight.’ Notice the word and falls before the tens-and-ones part — that is the NCERT convention Indian children are taught, and it is a small habit worth being consistent about.

Watch the tricky ones

Numbers with an internal zero trip children up when they write from words. ‘Four thousand and six’ is 4,006, not 46 or 4,600. The trick is to say which place each part belongs to: four thousands, no hundreds, no tens, six ones. Fill every seat, even the empty ones, with a 0.

The Indian comma: where it goes and why

In the Indian number system, the first comma in a four-digit number sits after the thousands digit — three places from the right. So one thousand two hundred and thirty-four is written 1,234, and the largest four-digit number is 9,999. Add one more and you reach 10,000 — five digits, and the start of ten-thousands, which is next year’s work.

Why bother with the comma at all? It groups the digits so the eye can read a big number at a glance without counting places one by one. Teach children to place it by counting three digits from the right and dropping the comma there. It becomes automatic fast.

A simple weekly routine that works

Ten minutes a day beats a marathon on Sunday. A rhythm I have seen work for parents in Tier-2 cities juggling jobs: two days naming the value of a chosen digit, two days on expanded form (both directions), one day writing numbers from words, and the weekend for mixed practice on paper. Use coins — a ₹1000 note, a ₹100, a ₹10 and a ₹1 — to make the four places physical. Money is the most natural place-value model there is, and it costs nothing to raid the piggy bank for a lesson.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free, eight-question quiz on exactly what we covered — naming places, the value of a digit, expanded form and reading four-digit numbers. Let your child work through it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 3 Place Value Quiz (up to 10,000)
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, expanded form and reading four-digit numbers. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 3 four-digit place value up to 10,000

questions.q: In the number 3,458, which place is the digit 4 in?
questions.explanation: Reading from the right: 8 ones, 5 tens, 4 hundreds, 3 thousands. So the 4 sits in the hundreds place.

questions.q: What is the value of the digit 7 in 7,041?
questions.explanation: The 7 is in the thousands place, so its value is 7,000.

questions.q: What is 6,205 written in expanded form?
questions.explanation: 6 thousands + 2 hundreds + 0 tens + 5 ones = 6000 + 200 + 5. The tens place is 0, so we leave it out.

questions.q: Which number is 'four thousand and six'?
questions.explanation: Four thousands, no hundreds, no tens, six ones. Fill the empty places with 0: 4,006.

questions.q: What is 7000 + 300 + 20 + 4 as a single number?
In 2,500 and 5,200, what is the digit 5 worth in each?
questions.explanation: In 5,200 the 5 is in the thousands, worth 5,000. In 2,500 the 5 is in the hundreds, worth 500. Same digit, different place, different value.

questions.q: What is the value of the 0 in 4,027?
options: It holds the hundreds place open
questions.explanation: The 0 is a placeholder in the hundreds place. Without it the number would be 427, which is different.

questions.q: Which is the largest four-digit number, just before 10,000?
questions.explanation: 9,999 is the biggest four-digit number. Add one more and you reach 10,000, which has five digits.

faq.q: What place value should a Grade 3 child know?
faq.a: By the end of Grade 3 a child should read, write and expand numbers up to 10,000, naming the thousands, hundreds, tens and ones places and giving the value of any digit by its place. This builds on the three-digit place value learned in Grade 2.

faq.q: How do I explain the value of a digit by its place?
faq.a: Use the same digit in two numbers. In 5,200 the 5 means 5,000; in 2,500 the same 5 means 500. Ask 'what is this digit worth?' about a fresh number each day until it becomes automatic.

faq.q: What is expanded form and why does it matter?
faq.a: Expanded form writes a number as the sum of what each digit is worth, so 3,458 = 3000 + 400 + 50 + 8. It makes place value visible and is the direct bridge to column addition, where thousands, hundreds, tens and ones are added separately.

faq.q: Where does the comma go in a four-digit number?
faq.a: In the Indian system the first comma sits three digits from the right, after the thousands digit — so it is written 1,234. Teach children to count three from the right and drop the comma there.
